before: Any car accident can cause serious harm, but few types of crashes are as violent or as dangerous as a rollover. When a vehicle flips onto its side or roof — sometimes multiple times — the forces inside the cabin are extreme, unpredictable, and often catastrophic. According to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), rollovers account for approximately 2% of all crashes but are responsible for nearly 30% of all passenger vehicle fatalities.
after: Any car accident can cause serious harm, but few types of crashes are as violent or as dangerous as a rollover. When a vehicle flips onto its side or roof — sometimes multiple times — the forces inside the cabin are extreme, unpredictable, and often catastrophic. According to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), only about 3% of passenger vehicles involved in crashes roll over, yet rollovers accounted for 28% of passenger vehicle occupant deaths in 2023.

before:
• Excessive speed — speed is a factor in nearly 40% of fatal rollovers; high speed increases the lateral forces during turns and makes recovery from a skid nearly impossible
  • Overcorrection — jerking the steering wheel after drifting off the road or during a skid is one of the most common triggers for a rollover
  • Distracted driving — a driver who drifts onto the shoulder while texting may overcorrect when they look up, initiating a rollover
  • Impaired driving — alcohol and drugs impair reaction time and judgment, contributing to the loss of control that precedes many rollovers
after:
• Excessive speed — NHTSA reports that about 40% of fatal rollover crashes involve speeding; high speed increases the lateral forces during turns and makes recovery from a skid nearly impossible
  • Overcorrection — jerking the steering wheel after drifting off the road or during a skid is one of the most common triggers for a rollover
  • Distracted driving — a driver who drifts onto the shoulder while texting may overcorrect when they look up, initiating a rollover
  • Impaired driving — alcohol and drugs impair reaction time and judgment, contributing to the loss of control that precedes many rollovers

before: The NHTSA reports that occupants who are ejected from a vehicle during a rollover are roughly 8 times more likely to be killed than those who remain inside.
after: According to NHTSA, the estimated 2022 fatality rate for occupants ejected from a vehicle during a rollover was 95.5%, compared with 4.7% for those who were not ejected. Belted occupants were 98% less likely to be ejected.

before:
• Another driver — if another vehicle caused the collision that triggered the rollover (e.g., sideswiping you, running a red light, cutting you off), that driver is liable for your injuries. This is the basis of a standard car accident or truck accident claim.
  • Vehicle manufacturer — if a design defect made the vehicle unreasonably prone to rolling over, or if the roof crushed in a way that worsened your injuries, the manufacturer may be liable under a product liability theory. Common defects include inadequate roof strength, faulty electronic stability control, and tire defects.
  • Tire manufacturer — tire blowouts caused by manufacturing defects or design flaws are a known rollover trigger
  • Government entity — if a road defect, missing guardrail, or inadequate signage contributed to the crash, the state or local government responsible for road maintenance may be liable. Claims against government entities in Georgia and South Carolina have special notice requirements and shorter deadlines.
  • Trucking company — if a commercial truck caused the rollover, the trucking company may be liable for improper loading, inadequate maintenance, or driver fatigue violations
  • Cargo loaders — improperly secured cargo that shifts during transit and triggers a rollover creates liability for the party responsible for loading

before:
• Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33): You can recover as long as you are less than 50% at fault. Your award is reduced by your percentage of responsibility.
  • South Carolina: You can recover as long as you are less than 51% at fault. Your award is reduced by your percentage of responsibility.

Seatbelt defense: The two states now take opposite positions. In Georgia, Senate Bill 68 revised O.C.G.A. § 40-8-76.1(d) effective April 21, 2025, so evidence that you were not wearing a seatbelt may be admitted on negligence, comparative negligence, causation, assumption of risk, or apportionment of fault, and may diminish your recovery. Georgia sets no fixed percentage reduction — the finder of fact apportions fault, and the court still weighs admissibility under O.C.G.A. § 24-4-403. In South Carolina the rule is the reverse: under S.C. Code § 56-5-6540(C), a seatbelt violation is not negligence per se or contributory negligence and is not admissible as evidence in a civil action. In neither state does going unbelted bar your claim.

before: If the at-fault party acted with gross negligence or reckless disregard — such as driving drunk or a manufacturer knowingly selling a vehicle with a rollover-prone design — you may recover punitive damages. Georgia caps punitive damages at $250,000 with exceptions for DUI and intentional conduct (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1). South Carolina caps them at the greater of 3x compensatory damages or $500,000 (S.C. Code § 15-32-530).
after: If the at-fault party acted with gross negligence or reckless disregard — such as driving drunk or a manufacturer knowingly selling a vehicle with a rollover-prone design — you may recover punitive damages. Georgia caps punitive damages at $250,000 (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1(g)), but there is no cap in product liability cases (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1(e); 75% of such an award goes to the state) or where the defendant acted with specific intent to harm or while substantially impaired by alcohol or drugs (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1(f)). South Carolina caps them at the greater of 3x compensatory damages or $500,000 (S.C. Code § 15-32-530).

before: If a rollover crash kills a loved one, surviving family members may file a wrongful death claim to recover funeral expenses, lost financial support, and compensation for the loss of companionship and guidance.
after: If a rollover crash kills a loved one, a wrongful death claim can recover funeral expenses, lost financial support, and compensation for the loss of companionship and guidance. In Georgia the surviving spouse, or the children if there is no surviving spouse, brings the claim (O.C.G.A. § 51-4-2). In South Carolina the executor or administrator of the estate brings it for the benefit of the surviving spouse and children, or if none, the parents or heirs (S.C. Code § 15-51-20).

before:
• Georgia: 2 years from the date of injury (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33)
  • South Carolina: 3 years from the date of injury (S.C. Code § 15-3-530)

If the rollover involved a government entity (e.g., a road defect claim), you may need to provide ante-litem notice much sooner — as early as 6 months to 1 year depending on the jurisdiction. Missing these deadlines can permanently bar your claim, which is why consulting an attorney promptly after a rollover crash is critical.
after:
• Georgia: 2 years from the date of injury (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33)
  • South Carolina: 3 years from the date of injury (S.C. Code § 15-3-530)

If the rollover involved a government entity (e.g., a road defect claim), the clock runs shorter. In Georgia, written ante-litem notice is due within 6 months for a city (O.C.G.A. § 36-33-5) or 12 months for a county (O.C.G.A. § 36-11-1) or the State (O.C.G.A. § 50-21-26). South Carolina's Tort Claims Act requires no pre-suit notice, but suit must be filed within 2 years (S.C. Code § 15-78-110), or 3 years if an optional verified claim was filed within 1 year (S.C. Code § 15-78-80). Missing these deadlines can permanently bar your claim, which is why consulting an attorney promptly after a rollover crash is critical.

Occupants suffer traumatic brain injuries, spinal cord damage, ejection injuries, and crush injuries. before: Rollover crashes subject occupants to violent multi-directional forces — throwing them sideways, upward, and downward in rapid succession. Occupants strike the roof, doors, windows, and dashboard repeatedly. If the roof crushes inward, survival space is reduced. Unbelted occupants face ejection, which increases the fatality risk by roughly 8 times according to NHTSA.
